To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

confidence intervals based on thresholding estimators in high-dimensional regression models are larger than the standard least-squares interval, and the asymptotic results for the known-variance model are valid also in the unknown-variance model if the degrees of freedom tend to infinity fast enough.

the coverage probability of the thresholded interval based on the hard-thresholding estimator in the known-variance Gaussian regression model is always at least 0.95, and that the coverage probability in the unknown-variance setting is always larger than 0.5.

confidence intervals based on thresholding estimators in high-dimensional regression are always larger than their least-squares counterparts, and the difference in size can be quite substantial in finite samples.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the thresholding-based confidence intervals can be used to provide a nonparametric and computationally cheap alternative to the standard confidence intervals when the number of regressor variables is large.

the coverage of confidence intervals based on thresholding estimators can be improved by using a smaller thresholding parameter, but this improvement comes at the expense of larger intervals and a loss of variable selection consistency.
, in the case where k is large and the thresholding estimations are tuned to perform variable selection, the intervals based the thresholding estimator are much wider than the standard interval.
